newsitem.title: UK: Wanted - experienced oil traders, pay no obstacle.
newsitem.headline: Wanted - experienced oil traders, pay no obstacle.

text.p: Booming business on the European oil trading scene has forced up salaries for key crude dealing staff as companies compete for a small pool of skilled traders.
The major players -- integrated oil majors and private trading companies -- are finding it increasingly difficult to land traders with the necessary experience, leading dealers said on Wednesday.

"The trouble is there hasn't been an inflow of junior traders over the last few years. It's just been the old names sitting around getting fat," one senior crude oil trader at a major European company said.
Surging North Sea crude output, a very volatile market and healthy profits last year have all contributed to the money to be made by those who trade oil.
"Everyone had a good year last year so there is plenty of money on the table....just not enough people for it," another trader said.
Top traders last year were reputed to have earned as much as a million pounds.
"This (price) volatility has brought lots of extra deals and interest into the market," said a crude dealer at an independent trading company.
"The funds and banks get involved on a more regular basis nowadays. More hands are needed to cover this volatility as well as the extra North Sea barrels."
The market news this week was that another two traders had moved jobs -- this time from Shell Trading and Shipping Company (Stasco).
Shell declined comment on the market in traders.
Both dealers are believed to have moved to one of the large international banks.
One trader with a major oil company said his company would need to change its practices to attract the talented traders now in such short supply.
"We are in danger of becoming a college after college and need to shape up and build incentive packages or we will lose people and find it very hard to hire," he said.
So far this year Amoco Corp and J.Aron (the trading arm of Goldman Sachs) have hired crude traders.

Still searching are Norway's Statoil, looking for two traders, British Petroleum, willing to train juniors and Swiss-based independent Vitol SA. J. Aron was looking to add to its team, traders said. Enterprise Oil has just hired.
A dealer with one of these companies said the going price for an experienced trader had soared in the past two years.
"We're up probably over 100 per cent," he said.
One major oil company, normally more conservative with salaries, was said to have offered in excess of 100,000 stg ($162,000) per annum for a trader with a few years experience.
A couple of years ago the figure would have been more like 40-50,000 stg.
Crude oil trading is now having to compete with the banking world on incentive schemes as well as basic salaries and bonuses.
Traders say some are offering sign-on fees of one year's salary.
"This has been going on in the banking world for a while but it's new for the oil market," another trader said.

Some of the majors, such as BP, run a bonus and share incentive scheme and with a fairly large group of experienced traders can continue to take in junior traders with limited experience and at relatively low salaries and train them up.
Some companies are examining their strategy both for finding qualified people and keeping them.
Statoil is among those trying to adapt to the new environment.

"We are reviewing our employment system and following the situation very closely in order that we can maintain the high quality service that is required in this tough world of trading," said John Ove Lindoe senior vice president of public affairs with Statoil.
